title: Allerleirauh
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 65. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, Thüre, Thier/Thiere, thust und ward).
about: The sixty-fifth tale in the Grimms’ collection (KHM 65), and one of the darkest openings in the book: a king, bound by a deathbed promise to marry no woman less beautiful than his wife, resolves to marry his own daughter. She plays for time with three impossible dresses and a cloak of a thousand furs, then flees by night and hides inside the fur as a kitchen drudge with soot on her face. The 1857 text does not soften the incest, and the name Allerleirauh — “all-kinds-of-rough,” of every sort of pelt — is left in German, since for most of the tale it is the only name she has.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein König, der hatte eine Frau mit goldenen Haaren, und sie war so schön, daß sich ihres Gleichen nicht mehr auf Erden fand.
sentences.l: There was once a king, he had a wife with golden hair, and she was so beautiful that her like was no more to be found on earth.
sentences.i: There was once a king who had a wife with golden hair, and she was so beautiful that her like was not to be found anywhere on earth.
sentences.n: “ihres Gleichen” = her equal, her like — a genitive. Where English says “was to be found,” German turns the verb reflexive: “sich fand.”

sentences.t: Es geschah, daß sie krank lag, und als sie fühlte daß sie bald sterben würde, rief sie den König und sprach „wenn du nach meinem Tode dich wieder vermählen willst, so nimm keine, die nicht eben so schön ist, als ich bin, und die nicht solche goldene Haare hat, wie ich habe; das mußt du mir versprechen.“
sentences.l: It came to pass that she lay ill, and when she felt that she would soon die, she called the king and spoke “if after my death you will marry again, then take none who is not just as beautiful as I am, and who has not such golden hair as I have; that you must promise me.”
sentences.i: It came to pass that she lay ill; and when she felt that she would soon die, she called the king and said: “If you mean to marry again after my death, take none who is not as beautiful as I am, and who has not golden hair such as mine. That you must promise me.”
sentences.n: The double negative is exact and it matters — “take none who is not just as beautiful” is the vow that will trap him. “eben so schön… als ich bin” uses als where modern German would use wie.

sentences.t: Nachdem es ihr der König versprochen hatte, that sie die Augen zu und starb.
sentences.l: After the king had promised it to her, she shut her eyes and died.
sentences.i: After the king had promised her this, she closed her eyes and died.
sentences.n: zuthun (modern zutun) = to close; the particle zu stands at the end. “that” is the 1857 spelling of tat.

sentences.t: Der König war lange Zeit nicht zu trösten und dachte nicht daran, eine zweite Frau zu nehmen.
sentences.l: The king was for a long time not to be comforted and did not think of taking a second wife.

sentences.t: Endlich sprachen seine Räthe „es geht nicht anders, der König muß sich wieder vermählen, damit wir eine Königin haben.“
sentences.l: At last his councillors spoke “it goes not otherwise, the king must marry again, so that we have a queen.”
sentences.i: At last his councillors said: “There is no help for it — the king must marry again, so that we may have a queen.”
sentences.n: Räthe = modern Räte, the king’s councillors. “es geht nicht anders” = there is no other way.

sentences.t: Nun wurden Boten weit und breit umhergeschickt, eine Braut zu suchen, die an Schönheit der verstorbenen Königin ganz gleich käme.
sentences.l: Now messengers were sent about far and wide, to seek a bride who in beauty would come quite equal to the dead queen.
sentences.i: Now messengers were sent out far and wide to seek a bride who should match the dead queen in beauty.
sentences.n: “gleich kommen” = to come up to, to match. käme is subjunctive: the bride is a wish, not yet a person.

sentences.t: Es war aber keine in der ganzen Welt zu finden, und wenn man sie auch gefunden hätte, so war doch keine da, die solche goldene Haare gehabt hätte.
sentences.l: But there was none in the whole world to be found, and even if one had found her, still there was none there who would have had such golden hair.
sentences.i: But there was none to be found in all the world; and even if one had been found, there was still none who had such golden hair.

sentences.t: Also kamen die Boten unverrichteter Sache wieder heim.
sentences.l: So the messengers came home again with the matter unaccomplished.
sentences.i: So the messengers came home again, their errand undone.
sentences.n: “unverrichteter Sache” is a fixed genitive phrase — “the business not done,” i.e. empty-handed.

sentences.t: Nun hatte der König eine Tochter, die war gerade so schön wie ihre verstorbene Mutter, und hatte auch solche goldene Haare.
sentences.l: Now the king had a daughter, she was just as beautiful as her dead mother, and had such golden hair too.
sentences.i: Now the king had a daughter who was just as beautiful as her dead mother, and had the same golden hair.

sentences.t: Als sie herangewachsen war, sah sie der König einmal an und sah daß sie in allem seiner verstorbenen Gemahlin ähnlich war und fühlte plötzlich eine heftige Liebe zu ihr.
sentences.l: When she had grown up, the king looked at her once and saw that she was in everything like his dead consort, and felt suddenly a violent love for her.
sentences.i: When she had grown up, the king looked at her one day and saw that she was in every way the likeness of his dead consort, and felt a sudden violent love for her.
sentences.n: heftig is a strong word — violent, vehement. Nothing in the sentence presents this as tenderness. Gemahlin is the elevated word for a wife, a consort.

sentences.t: Da sprach er zu seinen Räthen „ich will meine Tochter heirathen, denn sie ist das Ebenbild meiner verstorbenen Frau, und sonst kann ich doch keine Braut finden, die ihr gleicht.“
sentences.l: Then he spoke to his councillors “I will marry my daughter, for she is the very image of my dead wife, and otherwise I can find no bride at all who resembles her.”
sentences.i: Then he said to his councillors: “I will marry my daughter, for she is the very image of my dead wife, and I can find no other bride who is like her.”
sentences.n: Ebenbild is an exact likeness, an image — a heavier and more solemn word than Bild. The king offers it as his justification; the councillors answer by naming God.

sentences.t: Als die Räthe das hörten, erschraken sie und sprachen „Gott hat verboten daß der Vater seine Tochter heirathe, aus der Sünde kann nichts Gutes entspringen und das Reich wird mit ins Verderben gezogen.“
sentences.l: When the councillors heard that, they were horrified and spoke “God has forbidden that the father marry his daughter, out of the sin nothing good can spring and the kingdom is drawn along into ruin.”
sentences.i: When the councillors heard this they were appalled, and said: “God has forbidden a father to marry his daughter. Nothing good can spring from the sin, and the kingdom will be dragged down into ruin along with it.”
sentences.n: heirathe is subjunctive inside the reported prohibition. The mit in “wird mit… gezogen” is a stranded particle meaning “along with” — the realm goes down too. The councillors name the thing plainly, and the 1857 text does not soften it.

sentences.t: Die Tochter erschrak noch mehr als sie den Entschluß ihres Vaters vernahm, hoffte aber ihn von seinem Vorhaben noch abzubringen.
sentences.l: The daughter was frightened still more when she learned the resolve of her father, but hoped still to bring him away from his intention.
sentences.i: The daughter was more horrified still when she learned her father’s resolve, but hoped she might yet turn him from his purpose.
sentences.n: “jemanden von etwas abbringen” = to talk someone out of something; the separable ab shows plainly in abzubringen (ab-zu-bringen). vernehmen is a formal “to learn, to hear tell of.”

sentences.t: Da sagte sie zu ihm „eh ich euren Wunsch erfülle, muß ich erst drei Kleider haben, eins so golden wie die Sonne, eins so silbern wie der Mond, und eins so glänzend wie die Sterne; ferner verlange ich einen Mantel von tausenderlei Pelz und Rauhwerk zusammengesetzt, und ein jedes Thier in euerm Reich muß ein Stück von seiner Haut dazu geben.“
sentences.l: Then she said to him “before I fulfil your wish, I must first have three dresses, one as golden as the sun, one as silver as the moon, and one as shining as the stars; further I demand a mantle put together out of a thousand kinds of fur and pelt, and every animal in your kingdom must give a piece of its skin to it.”
sentences.i: Then she said to him: “Before I grant your wish I must first have three dresses — one as golden as the sun, one as silver as the moon, and one as bright as the stars; and further I require a mantle pieced together out of a thousand kinds of fur and pelt, and every animal in your kingdom must give a piece of its hide toward it.”
sentences.n: She addresses her father with euren, euerm — the respectful plural “you” a child uses to a parent, which English can no longer mark. tausenderlei = “of a thousand kinds.” Rauhwerk is a furrier’s word for rough pelts, and it is where her name will come from.

sentences.t: Sie dachte aber „das anzuschaffen ist ganz unmöglich, und ich bringe damit meinen Vater von seinen bösen Gedanken ab.“
sentences.l: But she thought “to procure that is quite impossible, and I bring my father thereby away from his wicked thoughts.”
sentences.i: But she thought: “Such things are quite impossible to come by, and so I shall turn my father from his wicked thoughts.”

sentences.t: Der König ließ aber nicht ab, und die geschicktesten Jungfrauen in seinem Reiche mußten die drei Kleider weben, eins so golden wie die Sonne, eins so silbern wie der Mond, und eins so glänzend wie die Sterne;
sentences.l: But the king did not leave off, and the most skilful maidens in his kingdom had to weave the three dresses, one as golden as the sun, one as silver as the moon, and one as shining as the stars;
sentences.i: But the king would not leave off, and the most skilful maidens in his kingdom had to weave the three dresses: one as golden as the sun, one as silver as the moon, and one as bright as the stars;
sentences.n: “ablassen” = to desist, to let up. Her three conditions come back word for word — Grimm’s formulas are meant to be heard twice.

sentences.t: und seine Jäger mußten alle Thiere im ganzen Reiche auffangen und ihnen ein Stück von ihrer Haut abziehen;
sentences.l: and his hunters had to catch all the animals in the whole kingdom and draw off from them a piece of their skin;
sentences.i: and his huntsmen had to catch every animal in the whole kingdom and strip a piece of hide from each;
sentences.n: abziehen is the butcher’s and furrier’s word: to flay, to draw the skin off. She asked for the impossible, and the king simply has it done.

sentences.t: daraus ward ein Mantel von tausenderlei Rauhwerk gemacht.
sentences.l: out of that was made a mantle of a thousand kinds of fur.
sentences.i: and from these a mantle of a thousand kinds of fur was made.

sentences.t: Endlich, als alles fertig war, ließ der König den Mantel herbei holen, breitete ihn vor ihr aus und sprach „morgen soll die Hochzeit sein.“
sentences.l: At last, when everything was ready, the king had the mantle fetched hither, spread it out before her and spoke “tomorrow shall the wedding be.”
sentences.i: At last, when all was ready, the king had the mantle brought, spread it out before her, and said: “Tomorrow shall be the wedding.”

sentences.t: Als nun die Königstochter sah daß keine Hoffnung mehr war ihres Vaters Herz umzuwenden, so faßte sie den Entschluß zu entfliehen.
sentences.l: When now the king’s-daughter saw that there was no hope any more of turning her father’s heart around, then she seized the resolve to flee.
sentences.i: When the king’s daughter saw that there was no hope left of turning her father’s heart, she took the resolve to flee.
sentences.n: “einen Entschluß fassen” = to take a decision — German grasps it. “ihres Vaters Herz” sets the genitive before its noun, an elevated order.

sentences.t: In der Nacht, während alles schlief, stand sie auf und nahm von ihren Kostbarkeiten dreierlei, einen goldenen Ring, ein goldenes Spinnrädchen und ein goldenes Haspelchen;
sentences.l: In the night, while everything slept, she stood up and took of her treasures three kinds of thing, a golden ring, a little golden spinning-wheel and a little golden reel;
sentences.i: In the night, while all lay sleeping, she rose and took three of her treasures — a golden ring, a little golden spinning wheel and a little golden reel;
sentences.n: A Haspel is the frame onto which spun yarn is wound off the wheel; both it and the wheel appear here as diminutives. Three tokens, one for each of the three feasts still to come.

sentences.t: die drei Kleider von Sonne Mond und Sternen, that sie in eine Nußschale, zog den Mantel von allerlei Rauhwerk an und machte sich Gesicht und Hände mit Ruß schwarz.
sentences.l: the three dresses of sun, moon and stars, she put into a nutshell, drew on the mantle of all kinds of fur and made herself face and hands black with soot.
sentences.i: the three dresses of sun, moon and stars she put into a nutshell; she drew on the mantle of every kind of fur and blackened her face and hands with soot.
sentences.n: The 1857 text prints “Sonne Mond und Sternen” without commas and sets one after Kleider where we would not; the punctuation stands as it is. “allerlei Rauhwerk” is the phrase her name is built out of.

sentences.t: Dann befahl sie sich Gott und gieng fort, und gieng die ganze Nacht, bis sie in einen großen Wald kam.
sentences.l: Then she commended herself to God and went away, and went the whole night, until she came into a great forest.
sentences.i: Then she commended herself to God and went away, and walked all night until she came to a great forest.
sentences.n: “sich Gott befehlen” = to commend oneself to God, an old formula spoken on setting out.

sentences.t: Und weil sie müde war, setzte sie sich in einen hohlen Baum, und schlief ein.
sentences.l: And because she was tired, she set herself down in a hollow tree, and fell asleep.

sentences.t: Die Sonne gieng auf und sie schlief fort und schlief noch immer, als es schon hoher Tag war.
sentences.l: The sun went up and she slept on and slept still, when it was already high day.
sentences.i: The sun rose, and she slept on and was sleeping still when the day was already well advanced.
sentences.n: “hoher Tag” = broad daylight, well into the morning.

sentences.t: Da trug es sich zu, daß der König, dem dieser Wald gehörte, darin jagte.
sentences.l: Then it came to pass that the king to whom this forest belonged was hunting in it.
sentences.n: “es trug sich zu” is the set phrase for “it came to pass.” This is a second king, not her father; the tale never names either of them.

sentences.t: Als seine Hunde zu dem Baum kamen, schnupperten sie, liefen rings herum und bellten.
sentences.l: When his dogs came to the tree, they sniffed, ran round about and barked.

sentences.t: Sprach der König zu den Jägern „seht doch was dort für ein Wild sich versteckt hat.“
sentences.l: Spoke the king to the hunters “do see what sort of game has hidden itself there.”
sentences.i: The king said to his huntsmen: “Go and see what kind of game has hidden itself there.”
sentences.n: The sentence opens with the verb — “Sprach der König” — a storyteller's inversion; the literal line keeps it, the idiomatic one rights the order. “was für ein” = what kind of. Wild is game, hunted beasts.

sentences.t: Die Jäger folgten dem Befehl, und als sie wieder kamen, sprachen sie „in dem hohlen Baum liegt ein wunderliches Thier, wie wir noch niemals eins gesehen haben: an seiner Haut ist tausenderlei Pelz; es liegt aber und schläft.“
sentences.l: The hunters followed the command, and when they came back, they spoke “in the hollow tree lies a strange animal, such as we have never yet seen one: on its skin is a thousand kinds of fur; but it lies and sleeps.”
sentences.i: The huntsmen obeyed, and when they came back they said: “In the hollow tree lies a strange beast, such as we have never seen: its hide has a thousand kinds of fur on it — but it is lying there asleep.”
sentences.n: wunderlich = strange, odd — not “wonderful.” The huntsmen take her for an animal, and from here on the text calls her es, “it,” for pages together: a grammatical neuter (das Thier, das Mädchen) that doubles as the loss of her name. Our idiomatic line says “she” where English cannot bear the “it.”

sentences.t: Sprach der König „seht zu ob ihrs lebendig fangen könnt, dann bindets auf den Wagen und nehmts mit.“
sentences.l: Spoke the king “see to it whether you can catch it alive, then bind it onto the cart and take it with.”
sentences.i: The king said: “See whether you can take it alive; then bind it on the cart and bring it along.”
sentences.n: ihrs = ihr es, bindets = bindet es, nehmts = nehmt es — the 1857 text clips the pronoun onto the verb wherever speech runs fast.

sentences.t: Als die Jäger das Mädchen anfaßten, erwachte es voll Schrecken und rief ihnen zu „ich bin ein armes Kind, von Vater und Mutter verlassen, erbarmt euch mein und nehmt mich mit.“
sentences.l: When the hunters took hold of the girl, it awoke full of terror and called to them “I am a poor child, forsaken by father and mother, have mercy on me and take me with you.”
sentences.i: When the huntsmen laid hold of the girl, she woke in terror and called out to them: “I am a poor child, forsaken by father and mother — take pity on me and bring me with you.”
sentences.n: “sich erbarmen” governs the genitive: “erbarmt euch mein” = have mercy on me, where mein is the old genitive of ich. Her plea is truer than the huntsmen can know, though it is her father she has fled.

sentences.t: Da sprachen sie „Allerleirauh, du bist gut für die Küche, komm nur mit, da kannst du die Asche zusammenkehren.“
sentences.l: Then they spoke “Allerleirauh, you are good for the kitchen, just come along, there you can sweep the ashes together.”
sentences.i: Then they said: “Allerleirauh, you are fit for the kitchen — come along, there you can sweep up the ashes.”
sentences.n: The name is coined on the spot: allerlei (all sorts) + rauh (rough, shaggy — the 1857 spelling of rau), so “all-kinds-of-rough,” all-kinds-of-fur. We leave it in German, since it is the only name she has for most of the tale.

sentences.t: Also setzten sie es auf den Wagen und fuhren heim in das königliche Schloß.
sentences.l: So they set it on the cart and drove home into the royal castle.
sentences.i: So they set her on the cart and drove home to the royal castle.

sentences.t: Dort wiesen sie ihm ein Ställchen an unter der Treppe, wo kein Tageslicht hinkam, und sagten „Rauhthierchen, da kannst du wohnen und schlafen.“
sentences.l: There they assigned it a little stall under the stair, where no daylight came, and said “little rough-beast, there you can live and sleep.”
sentences.i: There they assigned her a little stall under the stairs, where no daylight reached, and said: “Little Rough-Beast, there you can live and sleep.”
sentences.n: Ställchen is a diminutive of Stall, an animal’s stall — they house her as livestock. Rauhthierchen, “little rough animal,” is the kitchen’s name for her, and it sticks.

sentences.t: Dann ward es in die Küche geschickt, da trug es Holz und Wasser, schürte das Feuer, rupfte das Federvieh, belas das Gemüs, kehrte die Asche und that alle schlechte Arbeit.
sentences.l: Then it was sent into the kitchen, there it carried wood and water, stoked the fire, plucked the fowl, picked over the vegetables, swept the ashes and did all the mean work.
sentences.i: Then she was sent into the kitchen, where she carried wood and water, tended the fire, plucked the poultry, picked over the greens, swept the ashes and did all the meanest work.
sentences.n: belesen is an old kitchen word: to pick over greens, cleaning them leaf by leaf. Gemüs is the older form of Gemüse. schlecht keeps its older sense of “low, mean,” not “of poor quality.”

sentences.t: Da lebte Allerleirauh lange Zeit recht armselig.
sentences.l: There Allerleirauh lived for a long time quite wretchedly.

sentences.t: Ach, du schöne Königstochter, wie solls mit dir noch werden!
sentences.l: Ah, you beautiful king’s-daughter, how shall it yet go with you!
sentences.i: Ah, you beautiful king’s daughter — what is to become of you!
sentences.n: The narrator steps forward and speaks to her directly, the one time in the tale. solls = soll es; “wie soll es mit dir werden” = what is to become of you.

sentences.t: Es geschah aber einmal, daß ein Fest im Schloß gefeiert ward, da sprach sie zum Koch „darf ich ein wenig hinauf gehen und zusehen? ich will mich außen vor die Thüre stellen.“
sentences.l: But it happened once that a feast was celebrated in the castle, then she spoke to the cook “may I go up a little and look on? I will place myself outside before the door.”
sentences.i: But it happened one day that a feast was held in the castle, and she said to the cook: “May I go up a little while and look on? I will stand outside the door.”
sentences.n: zusehen = to watch, to look on. The 1857 text keeps her question mark inside the quotation and runs straight on with a lower-case ich; we keep the line as it stands.

sentences.t: Antwortete der Koch „ja, geh nur hin, aber in einer halben Stunde mußt du wieder hier sein und die Asche zusammentragen.“
sentences.l: Answered the cook “yes, just go there, but in half an hour you must be here again and carry the ashes together.”
sentences.i: The cook answered: “Yes, go along; but in half an hour you must be back here to gather up the ashes.”

sentences.t: Da nahm sie ihr Öllämpchen, gieng in ihr Ställchen, zog den Pelzrock aus und wusch sich den Ruß von dem Gesicht und den Händen ab, so daß ihre volle Schönheit wieder an den Tag kam.
sentences.l: Then she took her little oil-lamp, went into her little stall, drew off the fur coat and washed the soot from her face and her hands, so that her full beauty came to the day again.
sentences.i: Then she took her little oil lamp, went to her stall, drew off the fur coat and washed the soot from her face and hands, so that her full beauty came to light again.
sentences.n: “an den Tag kommen” = to come to light.

sentences.t: Dann machte sie die Nuß auf und holte ihr Kleid hervor, das wie die Sonne glänzte.
sentences.l: Then she opened the nut and brought out her dress that shone like the sun.

sentences.t: Und wie das geschehen war, gieng sie hinauf zum Fest, und alle traten ihr aus dem Weg, denn niemand kannte sie, und meinten nicht anders als daß es eine Königstochter wäre.
sentences.l: And when that had happened, she went up to the feast, and all stepped out of her way, for no one knew her, and they thought nothing other than that it was a king’s daughter.
sentences.i: And when this was done she went up to the feast, and everyone stepped out of her way, for no one knew her, and they took her for nothing other than a king’s daughter.
sentences.n: “nicht anders meinen als daß…” = to take it for nothing other than that. wäre is subjunctive — their assumption, not the narrator’s statement, though here the assumption happens to be true.

sentences.t: Der König aber kam ihr entgegen, reichte ihr die Hand und tanzte mit ihr, und dachte in seinem Herzen „so schön haben meine Augen noch keine gesehen.“
sentences.l: But the king came toward her, reached her his hand and danced with her, and thought in his heart “so beautiful have my eyes never yet seen any.”
sentences.i: But the king came to meet her, gave her his hand and danced with her, and thought in his heart: “My eyes have never yet seen any woman so beautiful.”
sentences.n: entgegenkommen (to come to meet) takes the dative: “kam ihr entgegen.”

sentences.t: Als der Tanz zu Ende war, verneigte sie sich, und wie sich der König umsah, war sie verschwunden, und niemand wußte wohin.
sentences.l: When the dance was at an end, she bowed herself, and as the king looked around, she was vanished, and no one knew whither.
sentences.i: When the dance was over she made her bow, and by the time the king had looked round she was gone, and no one knew where.

sentences.t: Die Wächter, die vor dem Schlosse standen, wurden gerufen und ausgefragt, aber niemand hatte sie erblickt.
sentences.l: The watchmen who stood before the castle were called and questioned, but no one had caught sight of her.

sentences.t: Sie war aber in ihr Ställchen gelaufen, hatte geschwind ihr Kleid ausgezogen, Gesicht und Hände schwarz gemacht und den Pelzmantel umgethan, und war wieder Allerleirauh.
sentences.l: But she had run into her little stall, had quickly drawn off her dress, made face and hands black and put the fur mantle round, and was Allerleirauh again.
sentences.i: But she had run to her stall, quickly drawn off her dress, blackened her face and hands and thrown the fur mantle round her — and was Allerleirauh again.
sentences.n: umthun (modern umtun) = to put round, to throw on; the th is the 1857 spelling.

sentences.t: Als sie nun in die Küche kam, und an ihre Arbeit gehen und die Asche zusammenkehren wollte, sprach der Koch „laß das gut sein bis morgen und koche mir da die Suppe für den König, ich will auch einmal ein bischen oben zugucken: aber laß mir kein Haar hineinfallen, sonst kriegst du in Zukunft nichts mehr zu essen.“
sentences.l: When she now came into the kitchen and wanted to go to her work and sweep the ashes together, the cook spoke “let that be until tomorrow and cook me the soup for the king there, I too want for once to peep a little up above: but let no hair fall into it on me, else in future you get nothing more to eat.”
sentences.i: And when she came into the kitchen and was about to set to her work and sweep up the ashes, the cook said: “Let that wait till tomorrow, and cook the king’s soup for me instead — I mean to go up and take a look for once myself. But mind you let no hair fall into it, or you will get nothing more to eat from now on.”
sentences.n: “laß das gut sein” = never mind that for now. bischen is the 1857 spelling of bißchen. zugucken is homely, colloquial — the cook does not talk like the court.

sentences.t: Da gieng der Koch fort, und Allerleirauh kochte die Suppe für den König, und kochte eine Brotsuppe, so gut es konnte,
sentences.l: Then the cook went away, and Allerleirauh cooked the soup for the king, and cooked a bread-soup, as well as it could,
sentences.i: Then the cook went off, and Allerleirauh cooked the soup for the king — a bread soup, as well as she could —
sentences.n: Brotsuppe is stale bread simmered in broth: poor people’s food, which is what makes the king’s delight in it worth telling.

sentences.t: und wie sie fertig war, holte es in dem Ställchen seinen goldenen Ring und legte ihn in die Schüssel, in welche die Suppe angerichtet ward.
sentences.l: and when it was ready, it fetched in the little stall its golden ring and laid it in the bowl into which the soup was served up.
sentences.i: and when it was ready she fetched her golden ring from the stall and laid it in the bowl into which the soup was served.
sentences.n: seinen is “its,” the neuter possessive agreeing with es rather than with the girl. anrichten = to dish up, to serve.

sentences.t: Als der Tanz zu Ende war, ließ sich der König die Suppe bringen und aß sie, und sie schmeckte ihm so gut, daß er meinte niemals eine bessere Suppe gegessen zu haben.
sentences.l: When the dance was at an end, the king had the soup brought to himself and ate it, and it tasted so good to him that he thought never to have eaten a better soup.
sentences.i: When the dance was over the king had the soup brought to him and ate it, and it tasted so good to him that he thought he had never eaten a better soup.
sentences.n: “es schmeckt mir gut” — in German the food tastes good to the person, and the eater stands in the dative.

sentences.t: Wie er aber auf den Grund kam, sah er da einen goldenen Ring liegen und konnte nicht begreifen wie er dahin gerathen war.
sentences.l: But when he came to the bottom, he saw a golden ring lying there and could not grasp how it had got there.
sentences.i: But when he came to the bottom of the bowl he saw a golden ring lying there, and could not conceive how it had come there.
sentences.n: Grund here is the bottom of the dish, not “reason.” gerathen (modern geraten) = to end up somewhere, usually by chance.

sentences.t: Da befahl er der Koch sollte vor ihn kommen.
sentences.l: Then he commanded the cook should come before him.
sentences.i: Then he gave order that the cook should come before him.
sentences.n: A reported command with no daß: the clause simply follows, and sollte carries the order.

sentences.t: Der Koch erschrack, wie er den Befehl hörte, und sprach zu Allerleirauh „gewiß hast du ein Haar in die Suppe fallen lassen; wenns wahr ist, so kriegst du Schläge.“
sentences.l: The cook was frightened when he heard the command, and spoke to Allerleirauh “certainly you have let a hair fall into the soup; if it is true, then you get blows.”
sentences.i: The cook took fright when he heard the order, and said to Allerleirauh: “You have surely let a hair fall into the soup; and if it is true you will get a beating.”
sentences.n: erschrack is the 1857 spelling of erschrak. wenns = wenn es. “Schläge kriegen” = to get a thrashing.

sentences.t: Als er vor den König kam, fragte dieser wer die Suppe gekocht hätte?
sentences.l: When he came before the king, this one asked who had cooked the soup?
sentences.i: When he came before the king, the king asked who had cooked the soup.
sentences.n: dieser, “this one,” points back to the last man named — the king — and keeps the two hes apart. The question mark stands although the question is reported, exactly as the 1857 text prints it.

sentences.t: Antwortete der Koch „ich habe sie gekocht.“
sentences.l: Answered the cook “I have cooked it.”
sentences.i: The cook answered: “I cooked it.”

sentences.t: Der König aber sprach „das ist nicht wahr, denn sie war auf andere Art und viel besser gekocht als sonst.“
sentences.l: But the king spoke “that is not true, for it was cooked in another manner and much better than usual.”
sentences.i: But the king said: “That is not true, for it was cooked in a different manner, and far better than usual.”

sentences.t: Antwortete er „ich muß es gestehen daß ich sie nicht gekocht habe, sondern das Rauhthierchen.“
sentences.l: Answered he “I must confess it that I did not cook it, but rather the little rough-beast.”
sentences.i: He answered: “I must confess that I did not cook it — the little Rough-Beast did.”

sentences.t: Sprach der König „geh und laß es herauf kommen.“
sentences.l: Spoke the king “go and let it come up.”
sentences.i: The king said: “Go, and have it come up here.”

sentences.t: Als Allerleirauh kam, fragte der König „wer bist du?“ „Ich bin ein armes Kind, das keinen Vater und Mutter mehr hat.“
sentences.l: When Allerleirauh came, the king asked “who are you?” “I am a poor child that has no father and mother any more.”
sentences.i: When Allerleirauh came, the king asked: “Who are you?” — “I am a poor child that has neither father nor mother any more.”
sentences.n: Her answer carries no speech tag at all; the 1857 text simply lets the second voice stand. It is a half-truth: her father is alive, and it is from him that she has run.

sentences.t: Fragte er weiter „wozu bist du in meinem Schloß?“ Antwortete es „ich bin zu nichts gut als daß mir die Stiefeln um den Kopf geworfen werden.“
sentences.l: Asked he further “to what end are you in my castle?” Answered it “I am good for nothing except that the boots are thrown at my head.”
sentences.i: He asked further: “What are you here for in my castle?” — She answered: “I am good for nothing but having boots thrown at my head.”
sentences.n: wozu = to what purpose. “mir die Stiefeln… geworfen werden” is a dative of disadvantage: the boots are thrown, and it is she who bears it. Whether the kitchen truly throws them, or she is simply saying what a drudge is worth, the tale leaves open.

sentences.t: Fragte er weiter „wo hast du den Ring her, der in der Suppe war?“ Antwortete es „von dem Ring weiß ich nichts.“
sentences.l: Asked he further “where have you the ring from that was in the soup?” Answered it “of the ring I know nothing.”
sentences.i: He asked further: “Where did you get the ring that was in the soup?” — She answered: “I know nothing of the ring.”
sentences.n: “wo… her” is one word pulled in two: woher, from where.

sentences.t: Also konnte der König nichts erfahren und mußte es wieder fortschicken.
sentences.l: So the king could learn nothing and had to send it away again.
sentences.i: So the king could learn nothing, and had to send her away again.

sentences.t: Über eine Zeit war wieder ein Fest, da bat Allerleirauh den Koch wie vorigesmal um Erlaubnis zusehen zu dürfen.
sentences.l: After a time there was a feast again, then Allerleirauh asked the cook as the previous time for permission to be allowed to look on.
sentences.i: After a time there was another feast, and Allerleirauh asked the cook, as before, for leave to look on.
sentences.n: “über eine Zeit” = after a while. vorigesmal is the older writing of voriges Mal.

sentences.t: Antwortete er „ja, aber komm in einer halben Stunde wieder und koch dem König die Brotsuppe, die er so gerne ißt.“
sentences.l: Answered he “yes, but come back in half an hour and cook the king the bread-soup that he so gladly eats.”
sentences.i: He answered: “Yes, but come back in half an hour and cook the king that bread soup he is so fond of.”
sentences.n: “gerne essen” = to like eating; German hangs the liking on the verb as an adverb rather than making a verb of it.

sentences.t: Da lief es in sein Ställchen, wusch sich geschwind und nahm aus der Nuß das Kleid, das so silbern war wie der Mond, und that es an.
sentences.l: Then it ran into its little stall, washed itself quickly and took out of the nut the dress that was as silver as the moon, and put it on.
sentences.i: Then she ran to her stall, washed quickly, took from the nut the dress that was as silver as the moon, and put it on.
sentences.n: “das Kleid anthun” (modern antun) = to put the dress on; the particle an waits at the end of the clause.

sentences.t: Da gieng sie hinauf, und glich einer Königstochter: und der König trat ihr entgegen und freute sich daß er sie wiedersah, und weil eben der Tanz anhub, so tanzten sie zusammen.
sentences.l: Then she went up, and resembled a king’s daughter: and the king stepped toward her and was glad that he saw her again, and because the dance was just striking up, they danced together.
sentences.i: Then she went up, and looked like a king’s daughter; and the king came to meet her and was glad to see her again, and because the dance was just striking up, they danced together.
sentences.n: anhub is the old preterite of anheben, to begin, to strike up (modern anfangen) — a form you meet in the older tales. gleichen takes the dative: “glich einer Königstochter.”

sentences.t: Als aber der Tanz zu Ende war, verschwand sie wieder so schnell daß der König nicht bemerken konnte wo sie hingieng.
sentences.l: But when the dance was at an end, she vanished again so quickly that the king could not notice where she went.
sentences.i: But when the dance was over she vanished again so quickly that the king could not see where she went.

sentences.t: Sie sprang aber in ihr Ställchen, und machte sich wieder zum Rauhthierchen, und gieng in die Küche, die Brotsuppe zu kochen.
sentences.l: But she sprang into her little stall, and made herself into the little rough-beast again, and went into the kitchen to cook the bread-soup.
sentences.i: But she ran to her stall, made herself the little Rough-Beast again, and went into the kitchen to cook the bread soup.

sentences.t: Als der Koch oben war, holte es das goldene Spinnrad und that es in die Schüssel, so daß die Suppe darüber angerichtet wurde.
sentences.l: When the cook was up above, it fetched the golden spinning-wheel and put it into the bowl, so that the soup was served up over it.
sentences.i: When the cook was upstairs she fetched the golden spinning wheel and put it into the bowl, so that the soup was served over it.
sentences.n: Earlier it was a Spinnrädchen, a little one; here it is the plain Spinnrad, and a few lines on the diminutive comes back. Grimm’s diminutives come and go with the telling.

sentences.t: Danach ward sie dem König gebracht, der aß sie und sie schmeckte ihm so gut, wie das vorigemal, und ließ den Koch kommen, der mußte auch diesmal gestehen daß Allerleirauh die Suppe gekocht hätte.
sentences.l: After that it was brought to the king, who ate it and it tasted as good to him as the previous time, and he had the cook come, who this time too had to confess that Allerleirauh had cooked the soup.
sentences.i: Then it was brought to the king, who ate it, and it tasted as good to him as the time before; and he sent for the cook, who this time too had to confess that Allerleirauh had cooked the soup.

sentences.t: Allerleirauh kam da wieder vor den König, aber sie antwortete daß sie nur dazu da wäre, daß ihr die Stiefeln an den Kopf geworfen würden und daß sie von dem goldenen Spinnrädchen gar nichts wüßte.
sentences.l: Allerleirauh came there again before the king, but she answered that she was only there for this, that the boots were thrown at her head, and that she knew nothing at all of the golden spinning-wheel.
sentences.i: Allerleirauh came before the king again, but answered that she was there for nothing but having boots thrown at her head, and that she knew nothing at all of the golden spinning wheel.
sentences.n: The second questioning is not played out in dialogue but folded into reported speech — hence the chain of subjunctives wäre, würden, wüßte.

sentences.t: Als der König zum drittenmal ein Fest anstellte, da gieng es nicht anders als die vorigemale.
sentences.l: When the king held a feast for the third time, it went no otherwise than the previous times.
sentences.i: When the king held a feast for the third time, it went just as it had the times before.

sentences.t: Der Koch sprach zwar „du bist eine Hexe, Rauhthierchen, und thust immer etwas in die Suppe, davon sie so gut wird, und dem König besser schmeckt als was ich koche;“ doch weil es so bat, so ließ er es auf die bestimmte Zeit hingehen.
sentences.l: The cook did indeed say “you are a witch, little rough-beast, and always put something into the soup, from which it becomes so good, and tastes better to the king than what I cook;” yet because it begged so, he let it go off for the appointed time.
sentences.i: The cook did say: “You are a witch, little Rough-Beast, and you always put something in the soup that makes it so good, and better to the king’s taste than anything I cook.” Yet because she begged so, he let her go for the appointed while.
sentences.n: The 1857 text sets the semicolon inside the closing quotation mark, and we keep it there. davon = “from which.” “hingehen lassen” here is simply to let her go off.

sentences.t: Nun zog es ein Kleid an, das wie die Sterne glänzte, und trat damit in den Saal.
sentences.l: Now it drew on a dress that shone like the stars, and stepped with it into the hall.
sentences.i: Now she put on a dress that shone like the stars, and walked into the hall in it.

sentences.t: Der König tanzte wieder mit der schönen Jungfrau und meinte daß sie noch niemals so schön gewesen wäre.
sentences.l: The king danced again with the beautiful maiden and thought that she had never yet been so beautiful.

sentences.t: Und während er tanzte, steckte er ihr, ohne daß sie es merkte, einen goldenen Ring an den Finger, und hatte befohlen daß der Tanz recht lang währen sollte.
sentences.l: And while he danced, he slipped her, without her noticing it, a golden ring onto the finger, and had commanded that the dance should last a good long time.
sentences.i: And while he danced he slipped a golden ring onto her finger without her noticing, having given order beforehand that the dance should last a good long while.
sentences.n: “ohne daß” = without someone’s doing something; German needs a whole clause where English can make do with a participle. anstecken, to slip a ring on, is separable: “steckte… an.”

sentences.t: Wie er zu Ende war, wollte er sie an den Händen fest halten, aber sie riß sich los und sprang so geschwind unter die Leute, daß sie vor seinen Augen verschwand.
sentences.l: When it was at an end, he wanted to hold her fast by the hands, but she tore herself loose and sprang so quickly in among the people that she vanished before his eyes.
sentences.i: When it was over he tried to hold her fast by the hands, but she tore herself free and darted so quickly in among the crowd that she vanished before his eyes.
sentences.n: “sich losreißen” = to tear oneself free. wollte here is “tried to,” not “wanted to” — the attempt fails as it is made.

sentences.t: Sie lief, was sie konnte, in ihr Ställchen unter der Treppe,
sentences.l: She ran what she could into her little stall under the stair,
sentences.i: She ran as hard as she could to her stall under the stairs,
sentences.n: “laufen was man kann” = to run as hard as one can.

sentences.t: weil sie aber zu lange und über eine halbe Stunde geblieben war, so konnte sie das schöne Kleid nicht ausziehen, sondern warf nur den Mantel von Pelz darüber, und in der Eile machte sie sich auch nicht ganz rußig, sondern ein Finger blieb weiß.
sentences.l: but because she had stayed too long and over half an hour, she could not draw off the beautiful dress, but only threw the mantle of fur over it, and in the haste she did not make herself quite sooty either, but one finger stayed white.
sentences.i: but because she had stayed too long — over the half hour — she could not get the beautiful dress off, and only threw the fur mantle over it; and in her haste she did not blacken herself thoroughly either, so that one finger stayed white.
sentences.n: Two small failures of haste, and both of them give her away: the dress beneath the fur, and the one clean finger.

sentences.t: Allerleirauh lief nun in die Küche, kochte dem König die Brotsuppe und legte, wie der Koch fort war, den goldenen Haspel hinein.
sentences.l: Allerleirauh now ran into the kitchen, cooked the king the bread-soup and laid, when the cook was away, the golden reel into it.
sentences.i: Allerleirauh now ran into the kitchen, cooked the king his bread soup, and when the cook was gone laid the golden reel in it.

sentences.t: Der König als er den Haspel auf dem Grunde fand, ließ Allerleirauh rufen: da erblickte er den weißen Finger und sah den Ring, den er im Tanze ihr angesteckt hatte.
sentences.l: The king, when he found the reel on the bottom, had Allerleirauh called: then he caught sight of the white finger and saw the ring that he had slipped on her in the dance.
sentences.i: The king, when he found the reel at the bottom, had Allerleirauh called; and then he caught sight of the white finger and saw the ring he had slipped on her in the dance.

sentences.t: Da ergriff er sie an der Hand, und hielt sie fest, und als sie sich losmachen und fortspringen wollte, that sich der Pelzmantel ein wenig auf, und das Sternenkleid schimmerte hervor.
sentences.l: Then he seized her by the hand and held her fast, and when she wanted to make herself loose and spring away, the fur mantle opened itself a little, and the star-dress shimmered out.
sentences.i: Then he seized her by the hand and held her fast; and when she tried to break free and run, the fur mantle fell a little open, and the star dress shimmered through.
sentences.n: “sich aufthun” (modern auftun) = to open, of itself. hervorschimmern is to shine out from behind something.

sentences.t: Der König faßte den Mantel und riß ihn ab.
sentences.l: The king took hold of the mantle and tore it off.

sentences.t: Da kamen die goldenen Haare hervor und sie stand da in voller Pracht und konnte sich nicht länger verbergen.
sentences.l: Then the golden hair came out and she stood there in full splendour and could hide herself no longer.
sentences.i: Then out came the golden hair, and she stood there in full splendour and could hide herself no longer.
sentences.n: Haare is plural in German where English uses “hair” as a mass noun. The golden hair is her mother's over again — the thing that set the whole tale in motion — surfacing here at the end.

sentences.t: Und als sie Ruß und Asche aus ihrem Gesicht gewischt hatte, da war sie schöner als man noch jemand auf Erden gesehen hat.
sentences.l: And when she had wiped soot and ashes out of her face, then she was more beautiful than one has ever seen anyone on earth.
sentences.i: And when she had wiped the soot and ashes from her face, she was more beautiful than anyone ever seen on earth.
sentences.n: The tense slips out of the past into “gesehen hat,” as anyone has ever seen — the teller stepping out of the story and into the room. It answers the first sentence, where the mother’s like was not to be found on earth.

sentences.t: Der König aber sprach „du bist meine liebe Braut, und wir scheiden nimmermehr von einander.“
sentences.l: But the king spoke “you are my dear bride, and we part nevermore from one another.”
sentences.i: But the king said: “You are my dear bride, and we shall never part from one another.”
sentences.n: nimmermehr = nevermore, an emphatic old “never.” Nothing is asked and nothing is explained; the courtship ends in a single line.

sentences.t: Darauf ward die Hochzeit gefeiert, und sie lebten vergnügt bis an ihren Tod.
sentences.l: Thereupon the wedding was celebrated, and they lived contentedly until their death.
sentences.i: Thereupon the wedding was held, and they lived in contentment until their death.
sentences.n: One of the collection’s closing formulas — plainer than the English “happily ever after,” and it names death.
